not_observable.reason: Which principal a downstream call actually carries is a runtime property. A shared service account named in configuration is reported; identity propagation working correctly is not observable from a repository.

Which principal a downstream call actually carries is a runtime property. Source shows the call being made; it does not show whose identity the token minted at run time belongs to, and nothing here infers one.

Tools defined only in code — an object literal passed to a framework, a decorated function, a registration call — are invisible to this adapter. It reads tool definitions published as JSON data and nothing else.

A tool whose name is computed — a template literal, a member expression, a config lookup — or whose definition is produced by a factory, spread into a registry, or handed to a wrapper shape outside this adapter's documented set, is reported as an unreadable construction with its line and is never given an invented name.

An inventory document states a policy; it does not enforce one. Where a policy is read from a document, the fact is marked inferred and says so, because a table row and an enforcement point are different things.

A `requiresApproval` flag in a definition object is a configuration value, not an enforcement point. Where one is read the fact is marked inferred and says so, because a boolean beside a tool and a gate in front of it are different things.

Whether a dispatcher resolves a tool name computed at run time is a property of the dispatcher, not of the manifest. Reported only where an execution sink over model-shaped input is visible in configuration.

Whether a dispatcher resolves a tool name computed at run time is a property of the dispatcher, not of a tool definition. This adapter reads definitions; it does not follow the dispatch path, and it reports neither that dynamic loading happens nor that it does not.

The input schema is recorded as a REFERENCE — the identifier the definition names, or the location of an inline literal. Resolving a schema across modules needs the type checker and a resolvable tsconfig, which ADR 005 defers with a trigger rather than building speculatively, so permissiveness is not observable here.

A JSON manifest does not say whether a tool can carry content out of the trust boundary. This adapter reports the capability only where a name or description asserts it, and never reports its absence.

Whether a tool can carry content out of the trust boundary is reported only where the definition states a send effect or names an outbound mechanism. Source that reaches the network through a helper this adapter did not follow is invisible to it, and its absence is never reported as evidence of containment.

A manifest names a tool; it does not classify what the tool does to the world. Side effects are reported only where the name or description states one, so a tool with a neutral name is `not_observable` rather than `read`.

A side effect is read only where the definition STATES one in a property. A definition that says nothing about what it does to the world is `not_observable` here, never `read` — `read` is the classification that agrees with a read-only contract and keeps a tool out of the destructive-action inventory.
